name: Attack and defence
goal: You can see which pieces each side attacks, take a piece that is left undefended, and save an attacked piece by moving it, guarding it, blocking or taking the attacker.

intro.text: A piece is attacked when an enemy piece could capture it on the next move. It is guarded, or defended, when one of your own pieces could take back if it were captured. If nothing guards an attacked piece, or the attacker is worth less than it (a pawn attacking a knight, say), you will lose it unless you do something. In this Lesson you take pieces your opponent leaves undefended, and you save your own in four ways: move the piece away, guard it, block the attack, or take the attacker.

parts.title: Take a piece nobody defends
parts.keyIdea: A piece that is attacked and not defended can be taken for free.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Black's knight has just taken your rook on g8. Look at that knight: is any black piece guarding it?

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: Nxg8+: your knight on f6 takes the knight on g8 (x means a capture, + a check). No black piece guards g8, so nothing can take back, and the capture even gives check to the king on h6.
The black king on g7 attacked your knight. The knight could jump to e7, f6 or h6, but f6 and h6 are next to the king, so e7 is the only safe square.

parts.title: Guard it
parts.keyIdea: When an attacked piece has no safe square, defend it with another piece.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are Black. White's king has just stepped to f4, where it attacks your rook on g5. Check every square the rook could move to before you decide.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: The rook had no safe square: on g4 the king takes it, and on f5 or h5 the g4 pawn does. So f6, the pawn one step forward, guards it instead. Now the white king cannot take the rook, because a king may never move to a square the enemy guards.

parts.title: Block the attack
parts.keyIdea: A bishop, rook or queen attacks along a line, so a piece put in the way blocks the attack.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Black's bishop has just moved to g5, and it attacks your rook on d2 along the diagonal. Look at the squares between the bishop and your rook.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: f4, the pawn from f2 to f4, steps into the bishop's diagonal, so the rook on d2 is no longer attacked. The pawn is safe there, because the g3 pawn and the rook on f1 guard it. It also attacks the bishop, so Black must spend the next move saving the bishop. Moving the rook would also have saved it, but then Black would not have had to spend a move on the bishop.

parts.title: Take the attacker
parts.keyIdea: The piece that attacks yours may be undefended itself; then the best defence is to take it.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Black's knight has just jumped to d6, where it attacks your knight on f5. Before you move your knight away, ask whether the attacker itself is safe.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: A knight that attacks a knight is attacked by it in return. Nothing guards the black knight on d6, so your knight takes it, and you are a whole piece up. Moving your knight away would also have saved it, but you would have missed a free piece.
